title: RDB: Relational Database
body: An RDB is a relational database that stores data in tabular form. Data is typically organized into a structure consisting of tables, rows, and columns.
when_to_show: When reviewing database, rdb, sql, table
detail: For example, you can create a student table, a problem table, and a solution record table, and link them together using IDs. RDBs have a clear structure and excel at conditional searches, sorting, and aggregation. However, changing the data structure may require a schema change. When reading code, RDBs are often mentioned alongside concepts such as SQL, primary keys, foreign keys, and joins.

title: NoSQL: A Database with a Flexible Structure
body: NoSQL refers to a method of storing data in various structures, not just traditional tabular databases.
when_to_show: When reviewing nosql, database, document_db, key_value
detail: Document-based databases can store data in document units similar to JSON, while key-value stores are well-suited for quickly retrieving values using keys. While NoSQL offers the advantage of flexible structure, it can become difficult to manage if data conventions become unclear. Therefore, you must consider the schema and validation rules together. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code.

title: Document DB: Stored as JSON
body: Document DB is a database that stores data in document units resembling JSON.
when_to_show: JSON, NoSQL, and Document Storage Issues
detail: While relational databases are centered around rows and columns in a table format, Document DB is more akin to a structure where multiple fields are contained within a single object. It is well-suited for data whose structure may vary slightly, such as study cards, user settings, and logs. However, just because the structure is flexible doesn’t mean you can store data haphazardly—doing so will make searching and validating data difficult later on, so it’s important to establish a schema and field conventions.

title: GraphDB: Focused on Relationship Exploration
body: A GraphDB is a database designed to store and retrieve data with a focus on exploring relationships. While traditional tables are row- and column-oriented, graph databases are node- and edge-oriented. For example, you can treat students, concepts, problems, and hints as nodes and connect them with relationships to show which students are struggling with which concepts. When reading GraphDB in code, you need to determine which node to start from and which relationships to follow. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you understand how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving a problem, first find the line in the code where this concept appears, and then categorize that line: is it a step that reads input, changes a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result? A GraphDB is a storage system that excels at navigating and exploring relationships between data. If a structure consists of interconnected documents, concepts, users, or tags, it can be interpreted as nodes and edges. When you encounter a GraphDB in code, you should determine which nodes are stored, which relationships are followed during a search, and what criteria are used to filter the results.
detail: GraphDB views data as nodes and edges and excels at traversing relationships. When you encounter GraphDB in code, first identify which objects are nodes and which connections are edges. By examining the direction of the relationships, the starting nodes, the traversal depth, and the result constraints, it becomes easier to understand recommendation systems and knowledge graph workflows.

title: VectorDB: Semantic Search
body: A vector database stores embeddings and metadata for sentences or document chunks, then finds items close to a query vector. An embedding is a numeric representation of text features, and similarity search compares the distance or similarity between those arrays. This can retrieve relevant text even when the wording differs, but it does not perfectly understand meaning or guarantee a correct answer. Read a RAG pipeline as ① splitting the source into chunks, ② creating embeddings with a compatible model, ③ storing vectors and source metadata, ④ running a top-k search, and ⑤ validating the retrieved evidence before adding it to the prompt.
detail: VectorDB is used to store text or documents as embedding vectors and to find items with similar meanings. When reading the code, break down the process into distinct steps: dividing the source text into chunks, generating embeddings, storing them, performing a top-k search, and feeding the search results into the prompt. You should also verify the source and score of the search results.

title: Index: An index for quick reference
body: An index is a tool for quickly finding data. Just like the index at the back of a book, it helps you jump directly to the information you need without having to search through the entire book from start to finish.
when_to_show: When reviewing index, database, search, performance
detail: In a database, creating an index on a specific field can speed up searches. However, indexes also require storage space and incur management costs. When reading code and encountering the term “index,” you must use context to distinguish whether it refers to a list index number or an index used to improve search performance. title: Schema: The Promise of Data
body: A schema is a set of conventions for data. It can be viewed as a set of rules that define which fields must be present, whether each field is a string, a number, or a list, and whether it is required or optional.
when_to_show: When reviewing schema, json, validation, database
detail: For example, if a “lesson” card must include “id,” “title,” “code,” “choices,” and “answer,” this is also part of the schema. When reading code, knowing the schema allows you to predict which keys are valid and what errors will occur if any are missing. This card is not just for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. A schema is a set of rules that defines which fields data must contain and what each field means.

title: ETL: Extract, Transform, Load
body: ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load, and refers to the process of retrieving, transforming, and storing data. Extract is the step of reading data from source files or APIs; Transform is the step of adjusting the format or selecting only the necessary fields; and Load is the step of storing the results in a database or file. Most Python batch scripts follow an ETL structure. When reviewing long code, it becomes easier to understand if you break it down by stage. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how specific variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line corresponds to reading input, modifying values, evaluating conditions, or storing or outputting results. ETL is a process for extracting, transforming, and loading data. “Extract” refers to reading from the source, “Transform” refers to cleaning and transforming the data, and “Load” refers to loading it into a database or file. When reading code, you should check the inputs and outputs of each step, how failed data is handled, and the methods used to prevent duplicates. This is the basic structure of a batch job.
when_to_show: When reviewing etl, harvest, transform, load
detail: ETL is a process that reads data from its source, transforms it into the required format, and stores it in a database or file. When reviewing long batch code, it becomes easier to understand if you break it down into its individual stages: Extract, Transform, and Load. You should verify the inputs and outputs of each stage, as well as failure handling, duplicate prevention, and re-execution safety.

title: Dedup: Duplicate Removal
body: "Dedup" refers to deduplication. If the same data is entered multiple times, statistics may be skewed, or users may see the same card repeatedly. To identify duplicates, criteria such as matching IDs, matching titles, matching normalized strings, or nearly identical content are required. In Python code, it is often associated with tools such as `set`, `dict`, `normalized key`, and `Counter`. When reading code, you should verify the criteria used to determine duplicates. This card is not just for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then categorize that line: is it a step that reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results? Dedup is the process of reducing the number of duplicate entries. You must define comparison criteria, such as title, URL, hash, or normalized text. When reading the code, you should verify what the criteria for determining duplicates are—whether only exact matches are removed or if similar entries are also grouped together. This directly affects data quality.
when_to_show: When reviewing dedup, set, hash, curation
detail: Deduplication is the process of reducing duplicate data. You must first define comparison criteria, such as the same URL, the same ID, normalized titles, or content hashes. When reviewing the code, check whether it removes only completely identical entries, groups similar entries together, and which entry is retained as the representative after determining duplicates. In some cases, selecting a representative item and documenting the rationale are more important than simply deleting data.

title: Metadata: Data that describes data
body: Metadata is data that describes other data.
when_to_show: When reviewing metadata, source, tag, filter
detail: For example, values such as the date a photo was taken, the source of a document, the difficulty level of a card, or the level of a lesson are not the original content itself, but rather information that describes that data. In a Python project, properly attaching metadata makes it easier to search, filter, sort, and validate the data later on. When reading code, you should distinguish metadata from the actual body of the code and verify what each value describes and where it is used.
